item.title: No salary, no vacation, no sick leave. But there are User Stories and Merge Requests: how AI agents work for me in Jira
item.description:
An IT team in a medium-sized company (product, integrator, it doesn't matter) usually consists of a product manager, business analysts, developers, and QA engineers. They typically work in one tracker like Jira. Now imagine that virtual colleagues have appeared in the Assignee field for all these roles. I have three of them: front-end, back-end, and analyst. They don't replace people. Reviews, answers to questions, and the final say in MR remain with the human, I'll show below where exactly. I give agents one-shot tasks: clear and limited enough to be solved in one pass without long correspondence. How it works in practice

item.title: I wanted to entrust AI with an entire project. I ran into issues with isolation, memory, and crash recovery
item.description:
What had to be checked before trusting a system with independent work on a software project. I wanted to build a system capable of independently managing a software project from idea to working product using AI agents. But the first engineering experiments showed that code generation is far from the most difficult part of the task. In the article, I discuss the development of Yggdrasil: why file system restrictions do not guarantee data protection, what problems remain after VM isolation, why memory limits do not provide strict guarantees for the host, and how to restore execution after failures without the risk of repeating actions already taken. I analyze real test results, including failed checks, adopted architectural decisions, and limitations that have not yet been overcome. The project is still in the research phase, so this is not about a ready-made solution, but about the problems encountered when trying to build truly autonomous AI development. Read more

item.title: A Day in the Life of G3A1SF: How I Train an Agent Without Backprop — It Lives by Day, Learns by Night
item.description:
What happens to an agent that doesn't solve one task but lives — for a long time, in a world that is constantly changing? I built NOWA-Cognitive, a cognitive architecture without backprop, without a global loss function, and without a language model in the decision loop: by day, the agent records experience quickly and "roughly," and rewrites long-term memory at night, during sleep. I'll explain how it works, using the example of one day in the life of a chinchilla from the colony — G3A1SF. Read on

item.title: Tom Wujec's Ideas on Engineering Creativity
item.description:
Or how to save a person working with a cognitive prosthesis. Long before the AI Cambrian explosion, Canadian designer Tom Wujec demonstrated the principles of engineering creativity through three simple exercises: the spaghetti tower with a marshmallow on top, drawing toast, and a sticker wall. His TED talks spread to training sessions and became educational materials for MVPs, pilot projects, system maps, and strategic sessions. Unfortunately, today these practices are often perceived as cargo cults, repeated as rituals: move a sticker, get a banana percentage of KPI. The theory, ideas, and history behind them are forgotten. If you've attended an Agile or Design Thinking training, you've likely seen many similar exercises. Four people, twenty dry spaghetti sticks, a yard of tape and string, one marshmallow, and eighteen minutes. The team argues, sketches, divides roles. A minute before the buzzer, the marshmallow is ceremoniously placed on top, and the structure slowly, with dignity, folds in half. Wujec, who conducted this exercise dozens of times, calls such a moment a transition from 'ta-da' to 'uh-oh.' Then, at the training, people usually laugh, discuss teamwork, and go for coffee. The exercise is done, the box is ticked. The idea it was meant to convey often remains on the table with the broken spaghetti. Wujec himself formulates it in one phrase: 'Every project has its own marshmallow.' This is an assumption that no one has tested and which will collapse the entire structure at the last moment. In modern development, such spaghetti towers are common, they just look different, and the marshmallow doesn't get any lighter. A model will generate code, a blueprint, or a hundred design options faster than a team can agree on who holds the tape. However, such code fails on the first live data. Wujec recently called artificial intelligence a wicked problem. But what lies behind this phrase? Luddism or a deep understanding of the fundamentals of the creative process? In this article, I will try to answer this question. To do this, I will dust off three of Wujec's talks and see what they laid the foundation for in modern business and IT. And I will also show that by returning to their essence, we get a ready-made way to work with AI. So, let's get out the record players, put on a Jethro Tull record, call your friends, and head to the kitchen for a pack of pasta. Read more

item.title: AI GM for Tabletop RPG: One Prompt Per Turn, Dice Before Response, and a Bug That Doubled Health
item.description:
I'm creating a browser-based text RPG where a language model acts as the Game Master. The player describes any action in their own words, the GM responds with a narrative, and the game handles the mechanics: health, money, stats, inventory, d20 rolls. It seems simple: send the model the story and character sheet, get a response. In practice, the most interesting challenges weren't in prompts like 'write humorously,' but at the intersection of a probabilistic model and deterministic game mechanics. Below are four such points and how I solved them. Stack: Node.js 24, Express, built-in node:sqlite, models via OpenRouter, and a shared engine module for server and browser. Read more

item.title: Interpretability of LLMs Proven?
item.description:
A preliminary report suggests that the impossibility of full LLM interpretability is overestimated. In his article on goodfire.com, author Nick Cammarata claims his experiments show that the formation of an LLM's response can be traced, allowing for changes in model training and verification approaches. The author himself calls the text a hypothesis, and the main article with a full description of the experiments is not yet available. However, as usual, a loud headline and strong claims have led to many retellings where the hypothesis has turned into a fact. Below is a quick look at the hypothesis. Read more

item.title: AI at Work: Workslop and How to Avoid It
item.description:
The problems with neural network efficiency are actually problems with how people interact with neural networks. And it's not the AI that needs "treatment"—it's improving your own competence: competence in working with AI, and, most importantly, your own competence in the work for which you use the neural network. Rest assured: if you don't understand the subject, the model will deceive you. Only real human experience will help you find and correct errors in time. An incompetent employee or manager won't know where to expect pitfalls, and the apparent, illusory competence of AI will only prolong the time until the error is realized, by which point it may have become systemic, and its consequences catastrophic. Read more

Original Russian article on Habr

item.title: Your secrets shouldn't go to the cloud: meet Obscura
item.description:
This summer, I wrote about what happens when you upload work data to ChatGPT: SOC logs, Cisco and FortiGate configs, internal IPs, employee emails. I then created an offline tool to clean configs manually before sending. It solves the problem for those who remember to use it. But a company cannot rely on everyone always remembering. So I took the next step: a gateway that sits between a person and a neural network, checks every request, and decides what to do with it. It's called Obscura. It works on-prem, so data stays within the network. How the gateway is built under the hood.

Original Russian article on Habr

item.title: A Play About On-Call Duty with an AIOps Agent. Inside: 340 Alerts, Three Bugs, and an "Abort" Button
item.description:
Night falls in the city, and the digital tech lead steps up for on-call duty. It stitches hundreds of alerts into a single incident, handles the first line of support, and writes post-mortems while the engineer finishes their coffee. It also suggests solutions, but sometimes they can make things worse. That's why the final decision always rests with the human in charge. We've staged one such week in the life of an AIOps agent as a five-act play. It features an on-call engineer named Alexey, his digital partner, and a restart button that hangs on the dashboard throughout the story, waiting for its moment. Alexey is a composite character. We didn't have to invent the late-night calls, the cold coffee, or the group chat where three teams fix one problem. Read on.
